summary: The stages of the system development life cycle and how the waterfall, agile and spiral models organise them.

theory.title: What the system development life cycle is

blocks.content: A structured sequence of **stages** that a team follows to **plan, build, introduce and maintain** a new information system. Each stage has clear activities and produces documents or products that the next stage uses.

items.title: Why follow an SDLC?
items.content:
- Breaks a large project into **manageable stages** with clear goals.
- Makes sure the system **meets the users' requirements**.
- Lets managers **plan time, cost and staff** and check progress at **milestones**.
- Produces **documentation** at every stage, so the system can be maintained later.
- Finds problems **early**, when they are cheaper to fix.

items.title: Who is involved?
items.content:
- **Client / end users** — describe their needs, test and use the system.
- **Systems analyst** — studies the current system and writes the requirements.
- **Designer** — plans the interface, data and processes.
- **Programmers / developers** — write the code and build the database.
- **Testers** — check that the system works and meets the requirements.
- **Project manager** — plans, schedules and controls the project.

blocks.content:
flowchart LR
  A[1 Analysis] --> B[2 Design] --> C[3 Development and testing] --> D[4 Implementation] --> E[5 Documentation] --> F[6 Evaluation and maintenance]
  F -. new requirements .-> A
blocks.caption: The six stages form a cycle — evaluation can start the next version

blocks.title: Same stages, different organisation
blocks.content: Every development model uses the **same stages**. What differs is **how they are organised**: done once in a strict order (**waterfall**), repeated in short cycles (**agile**), or repeated in loops driven by risk (**spiral**).
The analyst finds out **what the current system does, what is wrong with it and what the new system must do**.

blocks.title: Activities in the analysis stage
items: **Investigate the current system** using questionnaires, interviews, observation and examining documents.
Identify the **problems** of the current system and the **needs** of the users.
Identify **inputs, processes, outputs and storage** (often shown in a data flow diagram).
Carry out a **feasibility study** — is the project worth doing?
Produce the **requirements specification**, agreed with the client.

blocks.title: Feasibility study (TELOS)
rows: Do the hardware, software and skills exist to build it?
Do the benefits outweigh the costs? Is it within the budget?
Does it follow the law (e.g. personal data protection)?
Will the users actually be able and willing to use it?
Can it be finished by the deadline?

blocks.title: A requirements specification (extract) — online library
blocks.content:
1. The system must allow students to **search** books by title, author or ISBN.
2. The system must let librarians **record loans and returns** by scanning barcodes.
3. The system must **email a reminder** two days before a book is due.
4. A search must return results in **under 2 seconds**.
5. Only staff accounts may **edit** book records.
Requirements must be **specific and testable** — they are used again at the evaluation stage to decide whether the project succeeded.

theory.title: Stages 2 and 3 — Design, development and testing

blocks.content: The designer decides **how** the system will meet the requirements — before any code is written.

blocks.title: What is designed
rows: ERD, normalised tables, **data dictionary** (field names, types, sizes, validation rules)
Screen layouts, input forms, report layouts, **prototypes**
Validation rules, access levels, passwords, backups
**Test plan** with normal, boundary and erroneous data and expected results

blocks.content: Programmers **build** the system from the design: write the code, create the database, connect the interface. Testers then check it.

blocks.title: Kinds of testing
rows: Each module / function on its own
The whole system against the requirements
By the developers' own team, in-house, before release
By a limited group of **real users** in real conditions, before full release
By the **client**, to confirm the system meets the requirements before it is accepted

blocks.title: Test data
blocks.content: Each test uses **normal** (valid, typical), **boundary/extreme** (at the limits) and **erroneous** (invalid) data, recorded in the test plan with the **expected** and the **actual** result.

theory.title: Stages 4–6 — Implementation, documentation, evaluation and maintenance

blocks.content: The new system is **installed and put into use**: hardware and software are installed, existing data is **converted and transferred**, and users are **trained**. A changeover method is chosen:

blocks.title: Changeover methods
rows: Old system stopped, new one started at once
Both run together for a time; results compared
New system used in one part of the organisation first
New system introduced one module at a time

blocks.title: Two kinds of documentation
rows: The people who use the system
Program code with comments, algorithms, data dictionary, ERD/DFDs, hardware and software requirements, test results
How to install and log in, how to carry out each task, screenshots, error messages and what to do, FAQ, backup procedures, troubleshooting

blocks.content: The finished system is compared with the **requirements specification**: Does it do everything it should? Is it fast, reliable and easy to use? User feedback is collected; strengths, weaknesses and improvements are recorded.

items.title: Corrective
items.content: Fixing **bugs** found after the system is in use.

items.title: Adaptive
items.content: Changing the system to fit a **new environment** — a new OS, new law, new tax rate, new hardware.

items.title: Perfective
items.content: **Improving** the system — new features, better performance or interface, at the users' request.

blocks.content: "Name the stage" questions use key words: *feasibility, requirements* → **analysis**; *ERD, data dictionary, test plan, screen layout* → **design**; *coding, testing* → **development**; *training, data transfer, changeover* → **implementation**; *user guide* → **documentation**; *compare with requirements, bug fixes* → **evaluation and maintenance**.

A **linear, sequential** model: the stages are carried out **one after another, in a fixed order**. Each stage must be **completed and signed off** before the next starts, and the project does not normally go back to an earlier stage.

flowchart TB
  R[Requirements and analysis] --> D[Design] --> I[Implementation — coding] --> V[Testing] --> P[Deployment] --> M[Maintenance]
blocks.caption: Waterfall — each stage flows down into the next

items: Each stage produces **complete documentation** (requirements, design documents) before the next stage begins.
**Milestones** at the end of each stage make progress easy to measure.
The client is involved mainly **at the beginning** (requirements) and **at the end** (acceptance).
**Testing happens late**, after all the code is written.

blocks.title: Waterfall
rows: **Inflexible** — changing requirements later is difficult and expensive
Clear **structure**: a stage is completed before the next one starts
The client sees a **working product only at the end**
Each stage has **clear deliverables and milestones**
Errors in requirements or design are found **late**, during testing
**Cost and time** are easier to estimate
Long projects risk delivering a system that no longer fits the users' needs
Thorough **documentation** helps maintenance and new staff
Not suitable for complex projects where requirements are uncertain

blocks.title: When waterfall fits
blocks.content: A ministry orders a system to calculate a new tax: the rules are **fixed by law**, the requirements are clear from the start, and **detailed documentation** is required. Waterfall is suitable.

An **iterative and incremental** approach: the system is built in **short cycles (iterations or sprints)**, usually 1–4 weeks. Each cycle delivers a **working part** of the system, which the client reviews; the plan is adjusted after every cycle.

flowchart TB
  B[(Product backlog)] --> P[Sprint planning]
  P --> W[Design, build, test]
  W --> R[Sprint review with the client]
  R --> RE[Retrospective]
  RE --> P
  R --> S[Working increment of the software]
blocks.caption: Each sprint repeats plan, design, build, test and review

items.title: Roles
items.content: **Product owner** — represents the client, decides priorities. **Scrum master** — removes obstacles, keeps the process. **Development team** — designs, builds and tests.

items.title: Artefacts
items.content: **Product backlog** — prioritised list of all wanted features (user stories). **Sprint backlog** — the features chosen for this sprint. **Increment** — working software at the end of the sprint.

items.title: Events
items.content: **Sprint planning**, a short **daily stand-up** meeting (what I did, what I will do, problems), **sprint review** with the client, **retrospective** (how to work better).

blocks.title: A user story
blocks.content: "As a **student**, I want to **see my homework for the week** so that **I can plan my time**." The team estimates it, builds it in one sprint and shows it to the teacher at the review.

blocks.title: Agile
rows: Final **cost and deadline are hard to predict**
The client is **involved throughout** and gives regular feedback
Needs the client to be **available often**
**Working software early** — the most important features first
**Less documentation**, which can make maintenance harder
Needs an experienced, self-organised team; hard for very large teams

blocks.content: A **risk-driven, iterative** model (Barry Boehm, 1986). The project goes round a **spiral of loops**; every loop passes through **four phases**, and each loop produces a **more complete prototype** until the final system is built.

blocks.title: The four phases of each loop
items: **Determine objectives** — requirements and alternatives for this loop.
**Identify and resolve risks** — analyse what could go wrong (technical, cost, schedule); build a **prototype** or run a study to reduce the risk.
**Develop and test** — design, code and test the next version.
**Plan the next iteration** — the client **evaluates** the result; decide whether and how to continue.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  O[1 Objectives] --> R[2 Risk analysis + prototype]
  R --> D[3 Develop and test]
  D --> P[4 Evaluate and plan]
  P -- next loop --> O
  P -- complete --> F([Final system])
blocks.caption: Every loop passes through the four phases; each new loop builds a more complete version

blocks.title: Example — three loops for an online banking app
rows: Will customers understand and accept the idea?
Paper/screen **prototype** of the main screens, approved by the client
Is the payment process secure and fast enough?
Working prototype of log-in and payments, security tested
Can the system handle thousands of users at once?

blocks.title: Spiral
rows: **Risk analysis in every loop** — high-risk problems found early
Suitable for **large, complex and high-risk** projects
The number of loops — and so the end date — is uncertain
Requirements can be refined in each loop
Changes can be added in later loops
Success depends heavily on good risk analysis

blocks.title: Waterfall vs agile vs spiral
rows: At the end of each loop
Small/medium projects with clear, stable requirements
Projects with changing requirements and an available client

blocks.title: Choosing a model for a scenario
rows: A school library system; the requirements are fully known and will not change
Clear requirements; simple to manage and document
A start-up's mobile app; features change after users try each version
Frequent change and feedback; early releases
A new air-traffic control or banking payment system
Very high risk and cost; risk analysis in every loop
A government system whose rules are set by law and need full documentation
A school app for teachers who want to see each feature and suggest changes

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name two benefits of using a waterfall model. [2]**
1. It has a **clear structure** — each stage is **completed before** the next begins.
2. It is **easy to manage**, with **clear milestones** and documentation for every stage.

**Q: Explain one disadvantage of the agile model for a client. [2]**
The client must **take part in reviews regularly** throughout the project (1), **which takes up a lot of their time** / and the final cost is hard to predict because requirements keep changing (1).

**Q: Explain why the spiral model is suitable for developing software for a bank. [2]**
The project is **high-risk and expensive** (1), and the spiral model **analyses and reduces risks in every loop** using prototypes before the full system is built (1).

- Saying agile has **no** planning or documentation — it has **less**, and plans each sprint.
- Confusing **prototyping** with agile: prototypes are used in several models (especially spiral).
- Giving an advantage without linking it to the **scenario** when the question describes one.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: List the six SDLC stages in order and one output of each.
What does each letter of TELOS stand for?
What is the difference between alpha, beta and acceptance testing?
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each model.
Which model would you choose for a project with very high risk? Why?

questions.title: Order of SDLC stages
questions.text: Which sequence shows the stages of the system development life cycle in the correct order?

content.hint: You must understand the problem before you can plan a solution.

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: The problem is investigated (analysis) before the solution is planned (design), built (development), checked (testing) and installed (implementation).

questions.title: Output of the analysis stage
questions.text: State the main document produced at the end of the **analysis** stage.

content.hint: It lists what the new system must do.

scheme.mark_scheme: Requirements specification (accept: system requirements / requirements document / user requirements).
scheme.model_answer: A requirements specification.
scheme.explanation: Analysis investigates the problem and records what the new system must do in a requirements specification, which is the input to the design stage.

questions.title: Match stages to activities
questions.text: Match each SDLC stage to the activity that takes place in it.

right.text: Interviewing users and observing the current system
Producing input screen layouts and data structures
Running the program with normal, boundary and erroneous data
Changing the system after it is in use to fix newly found errors

scheme.mark_scheme: Analysis–R1, Design–R2, Testing–R3, Maintenance–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Agile and requirements
questions.text: In the agile model, all requirements must be fixed and signed off before any code is written.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Fixed, signed-off requirements are a feature of the waterfall model. Agile expects requirements to change and adapts the plan after each iteration.

questions.title: Distinctive feature of the spiral model
questions.text: Which feature most clearly distinguishes the spiral model from the other development models?

options.content: It produces working software at the end of each sprint
It completes each stage fully before moving on
It includes a risk-analysis phase in every iteration
It does not require any documentation

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: Risk analysis in each loop is the defining characteristic of the spiral model.

questions.title: Disadvantages of waterfall
questions.text: Select **two** disadvantages of the waterfall model.

options.content: The client does not see a working system until late in the project
Changes to requirements during development are difficult and costly

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Explain an advantage of agile
questions.text: Explain **one** advantage of using the agile model rather than the waterfall model.

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 mark for identifying an advantage; 1 mark for explaining why it is an advantage / how it arises.

Examples:
- Can respond to changing requirements (1) because the plan is reviewed after each short iteration (1).
- Client sees working parts early (1) so misunderstandings are found and corrected before much time/money is wasted (1).
- Working parts can be used before the project ends (1) because each iteration delivers a usable increment (1).

points.criterion: Identifies a valid advantage of agile over waterfall
Explains why/how this advantage arises (expansion linked to iterations or client feedback)

scheme.model_answer: Agile can cope with changing requirements, because the system is built in short iterations and the client reviews each one, so new or changed requirements can be included in the next iteration instead of having to restart the project.
scheme.ai_instructions: Award the second mark only if the expansion explains the mechanism (short iterations, regular client feedback, incremental delivery). A second advantage without expansion does not earn the second mark.

questions.title: Choose a model for a hospital system
questions.text:
A hospital is commissioning a large system that controls the dosage of medicines given to patients. The system is expensive to build and errors could endanger lives. Some requirements are not yet fully understood.

Discuss which development model (waterfall, agile or spiral) is most suitable for this project. Justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks. Expected choice: **spiral** (accept a well-justified alternative, maximum 3 marks).

- Identifies spiral as most suitable (1)
- Justification linked to risk: risk analysis in every loop reduces the danger of errors in a safety-critical system (1)
- Justification linked to size/cost: suitable for large, expensive projects (1)
- Justification linked to unclear requirements: prototypes/iterations allow requirements to be refined (1)
- Comparison point: why waterfall (fixed requirements) or agile (less up-front risk analysis/documentation) is less suitable (1)

points.criterion: Chooses the spiral model (or a justified alternative)
Links risk analysis to the safety-critical nature of the system
Links model to the large/expensive scale of the project
Links iterations/prototypes to the requirements that are not fully understood
Explains why another model is less suitable

scheme.model_answer: The spiral model is most suitable. Because errors could endanger patients, the risk-analysis phase in every loop means hazards are identified and reduced before each new part is built. The project is large and expensive, which is the kind of project spiral is designed for. As some requirements are unclear, each loop can produce a prototype that doctors evaluate, refining the requirements. Waterfall would be unsuitable because it needs all requirements fixed at the start, and agile performs less formal risk analysis and documentation, which a safety-critical system needs.
scheme.ai_instructions: Maximum 4 marks. Points must be applied to the hospital scenario; generic statements about a model that are not linked to the scenario earn at most 1 mark in total. If the student chooses agile or waterfall, award a maximum of 3 marks for justification that is accurate and linked to the scenario.
scheme.explanation: A 'discuss' question needs a decision and justification applied to the context, ideally with a counter-point about the alternatives.

questions.title: Define the SDLC
questions.text: Define the term **system development life cycle (SDLC)**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A structured sequence of stages / steps (1)
- followed to plan, develop, implement and maintain a (new) information system (1)

points.criterion: Used to plan, build, introduce and maintain a system

scheme.model_answer: A structured sequence of stages that is followed to plan, build, introduce and maintain a new information system.
scheme.explanation: The SDLC breaks a project into stages — analysis, design, development and testing, implementation, documentation, evaluation and maintenance.

questions.title: When is a feasibility study done?
questions.text: In which stage of the SDLC is a **feasibility study** carried out?

scheme.mark_scheme: B — Analysis (1)
scheme.explanation: The feasibility study is part of analysis: before designing anything, the team checks that the project is technically, economically, legally, operationally and schedule-wise possible.

questions.title: Types of feasibility (TELOS)
questions.text: Match each type of feasibility to the question it answers.

right.text: Do the hardware, software and skills exist to build it?
Do the benefits outweigh the costs?
Does it comply with laws such as data protection?
Will the users be able and willing to use it?
Can it be finished by the deadline?

scheme.mark_scheme: Technical → hardware/software/skills exist; Economic → benefits outweigh costs; Legal → follows the law; Operational → users able and willing to use it; Schedule → finished by the deadline (1 each)
scheme.explanation: TELOS = Technical, Economic, Legal, Operational, Schedule.

questions.title: Design-stage documents
questions.text: Select **three** documents that are produced during the **design** stage.

scheme.mark_scheme: A, B, D (1 each)
scheme.explanation: ERDs, the data dictionary and the test plan are design documents. The feasibility report belongs to analysis, the user guide to documentation, and the evaluation report to evaluation.

questions.title: Name the stage
questions.text:
Complete the sentences with the name of the SDLC stage.

The analyst interviews users and studies documents of the current system during the [[1]] stage. The ERD and the data dictionary are produced during the [[2]] stage. Users are trained and existing data is transferred during the [[3]] stage.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) analysis (2) design (3) implementation
scheme.explanation: Analysis investigates the current system; design produces the plans (ERD, data dictionary, layouts); implementation installs the system, transfers data and trains users.

questions.title: Alpha, beta and acceptance testing
questions.text: Match each kind of testing to its description.

right.text: Carried out in-house by the developers' own team
A limited group of real users tries the system before full release
The client checks that the system meets the requirements before accepting it

scheme.mark_scheme: Alpha → developers' own team in-house; Beta → limited group of real users before full release; Acceptance → the client confirms requirements are met (1 each)
scheme.explanation: Alpha testing is in-house, beta testing uses real users before release, acceptance testing is done by the client to accept the system.

questions.title: Types of maintenance
questions.text: Complete the table with the type of maintenance (**corrective**, **adaptive** or **perfective**) for each change.

prefill: A bug that crashes the report screen is fixed
The system is updated because the tax rate was changed by law
A new export-to-PDF feature is added at the users' request

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 Corrective (1)
2 Adaptive (1)
3 Perfective (1)

points.criterion: New feature requested by users → perfective

scheme.explanation: Corrective fixes errors; adaptive changes the system for a new environment (law, OS, hardware); perfective improves or adds features.

questions.title: Technical vs user documentation
questions.text: State **one** item that is included in **technical** documentation and **one** item that is included in **user** documentation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Technical (1): program code / comments, algorithms or flowcharts, data dictionary, ERD/DFD, hardware and software requirements, test results

User (1): how to install / log in, how to carry out tasks, screenshots, error messages and what to do, FAQ / troubleshooting, backup procedures
scheme.model_answer: Technical: the data dictionary. User: step-by-step instructions on how to log in.
scheme.ai_instructions: Each box is marked separately; the item must belong to that type of documentation.

questions.title: Why the requirements are used in evaluation
questions.text: Explain why the **requirements specification** is used again in the **evaluation** stage.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The finished system is compared against the requirements (1)
- to decide whether it does everything it should / whether the project succeeded / to identify improvements (1)

points.criterion: The system is compared with the requirements
To check whether all requirements are met / project succeeded / find improvements

scheme.model_answer: The new system is compared with each requirement in the specification to decide whether it meets the client's needs and what still needs to be improved.
scheme.explanation: Specific, testable requirements make evaluation objective.

questions.title: Testing in the waterfall model
questions.text: In the waterfall model, testing usually takes place only after all of the code has been written.

scheme.mark_scheme: True (1)
scheme.explanation: Waterfall is sequential: implementation (coding) is completed before the testing stage starts, so errors are often found late.

questions.title: Benefits of the waterfall model
questions.text: Name **two** benefits of using the waterfall model.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): clear / simple structure; each stage is completed before the next starts; easy to manage with clear milestones; cost and time easy to estimate; thorough documentation at each stage; suitable when requirements are clear and fixed
scheme.model_answer: 1 Clear structure — each stage is completed before the next begins. 2 Cost and time are easier to estimate.
scheme.ai_instructions: Do not credit the same benefit twice.

questions.title: Scrum roles and events
questions.text: Match each Scrum term to its description.

right.text: Represents the client and decides which features have priority
Helps the team follow the process and removes obstacles
A short cycle of 1–4 weeks that delivers working software
A short meeting every day about progress and problems

scheme.mark_scheme: Product owner → decides priorities for the client; Scrum master → removes obstacles; Sprint → 1–4 week cycle producing working software; Daily stand-up → short daily meeting (1 each)
scheme.explanation: Scrum is an agile method: work is done in sprints; the product owner prioritises the backlog; the scrum master keeps the process running; the team meets briefly every day.

questions.title: What a sprint delivers
questions.text: What is produced at the end of each sprint in the agile model?

scheme.explanation: Each sprint delivers a working increment that the client reviews; the final system is built up over many sprints.

options.content: A working part (increment) of the software

questions.title: A disadvantage of agile for the client
questions.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of the agile model for the **client**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one explained point (2): the client must attend reviews regularly (1) which takes a lot of their time (1); requirements keep changing (1) so the final cost / deadline is hard to predict (1); less documentation (1) so later maintenance may be harder / more expensive (1)

points.criterion: Explains its consequence for the client

scheme.model_answer: The client has to take part in a review at the end of every sprint, which takes up a lot of their time over the whole project.
scheme.ai_instructions: The second mark needs a consequence linked to the client.

questions.title: Phases of the spiral model
questions.text:
Complete the description of one loop of the spiral model.

Each loop has four phases: determine the [[1]], identify and resolve the [[2]], develop and [[3]] the next version, and [[4]] the next iteration after the client's evaluation.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) objectives (2) risks (3) test (4) plan
scheme.explanation: Objectives → risk analysis (often with a prototype) → develop and test → evaluate and plan the next loop.

questions.title: Spiral model for a small project
questions.text: Explain why the spiral model is **not** usually a good choice for a small, low-risk project.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Risk analysis in every loop is expensive / needs specialists (1)
- which is not worth the cost when the project is small / risks are low (1)
- the process is complex to manage / many loops for a simple system (1)

Max 2

points.criterion: Risk analysis / loops are expensive or complex
Not justified for a small, low-risk project

scheme.model_answer: Each loop needs a risk analysis carried out by specialists, which is expensive and complex; for a small, low-risk project that cost is not justified, so a simpler model such as waterfall is better.

questions.title: Which model is it?
questions.text: Tick **one** box in each row to show which development model the statement describes best. Leave the other boxes empty.

prefill: Risk analysis is carried out in every loop
All requirements are fixed at the start
Working software is delivered every 1–4 weeks
Each stage is signed off before the next begins

scheme.mark_scheme: Risk analysis in every loop → Spiral; Requirements fixed at the start → Waterfall; Working software every 1–4 weeks → Agile; Each stage signed off before the next → Waterfall (1 per row)
scheme.explanation: Spiral is risk-driven, agile delivers in sprints, waterfall fixes requirements and completes stages in order.

questions.title: Choosing a model for a start-up
questions.text: A start-up is building a mobile app. The founders expect the features to change after users try each version. Which development model is most suitable?

scheme.mark_scheme: B — Agile (1)
scheme.explanation: Agile handles changing requirements through short sprints with regular feedback from users.

options.content: None — the app should be written without a model

questions.title: Waterfall or agile for a timetable system
questions.text:
A school wants an online timetable system. The deputy head can only describe some of the requirements now; teachers want to try early versions and suggest changes.

Compare the **waterfall** and **agile** models for this project and recommend which one the developers should use. Justify your recommendation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Waterfall points (max 2): simple to manage, clear milestones, good documentation (1); but requirements must be fixed at the start / changes are hard (1); teachers would only see the system at the end (1)

Agile points (max 2): requirements can change between sprints (1); teachers see and test working versions early and give feedback (1); final cost and time less predictable / needs teachers' time (1)

Recommendation (max 2): agile (1) because requirements are incomplete and teachers want to try versions and suggest changes (1)

points.criterion: Second valid point about waterfall (advantage or disadvantage)

scheme.model_answer: Waterfall is easy to manage and well documented, but it needs all requirements fixed at the start and teachers would only see the system at the end. Agile lets requirements change between sprints and gives teachers working versions to test early, although its final cost and deadline are harder to predict. Agile is recommended, because the deputy head cannot describe all the requirements yet and teachers want to try early versions and suggest changes.
scheme.ai_instructions: Credit comparisons that refer to both models. The justification mark must use the scenario (incomplete requirements / teacher feedback). Waterfall can only earn the recommendation mark if strongly justified from the scenario — it is not the expected answer.

questions.title: A new system for a city library
questions.text: A city library still records loans on paper cards. The director wants a computerised system. The requirements are **clear and are not expected to change**, the budget is fixed, and the project is **low-risk**.

parts.title: Collecting information
parts.text: State **two** methods the analyst could use to collect information about the current paper system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): interviews (with librarians / director); questionnaires (to readers / staff); observation of staff issuing books; examining documents (loan cards, records)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Interviewing the librarians. 2 Examining the existing paper loan cards.

parts.title: Why a feasibility study
parts.text: Explain why a **feasibility study** should be carried out before the new system is designed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- To check whether the project is possible / worth doing (technically, economically, legally, operationally, within the schedule) (1)
- so that money and time are not wasted on a project that cannot succeed / to decide whether to go ahead (1)

points.criterion: Checks whether the project is possible / worthwhile
Avoids wasting time and money / supports the decision to proceed

scheme.model_answer: It checks whether the system can be built within the library's budget, time and legal limits, so the director does not waste money on a project that cannot succeed.

parts.title: Testing by the library
parts.text: The library staff test the finished system to confirm that it meets their requirements before they accept it. What is this type of testing called?

scheme.mark_scheme: C — acceptance testing (1)
scheme.explanation: Acceptance testing is done by the client before accepting the system.

parts.title: Choosing a model for the library
parts.text: Suggest whether the **waterfall** model or the **spiral** model is more suitable for this project. Justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Waterfall (1)
- requirements are clear and fixed, so a sequential model works / changes are not expected (1)
- the project is low-risk / small budget, so spiral's risk analysis in every loop would be unnecessary and expensive (1)

points.criterion: Justification: low risk / fixed budget makes spiral's risk analysis unnecessary

scheme.model_answer: Waterfall, because the library's requirements are clear and will not change, so stages can be completed in order; the project is low-risk with a fixed budget, so the expensive risk analysis of the spiral model is not needed.
scheme.ai_instructions: Justification marks must refer to the scenario.

questions.title: School canteen pre-order system
questions.text: A school canteen takes lunch orders on paper forms. Queues are long and orders are often lost. The principal hires a software developer to create an **online pre-order system**, following the stages of the system development life cycle.

parts.title: SDLC exam 1a
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the stage of the system development life cycle in which the developer carries out each activity.

prefill: Interviewing canteen staff about how orders are taken now
Drawing the layout of the order screen
Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data
Training canteen staff to use the system

scheme.mark_scheme:
Interviewing staff → Analysis; Feasibility report → Analysis; Order screen layout → Design; Writing program code → Development and testing; Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data → Development and testing; Training staff → Implementation

Six rows correct (3); four or five (2); two or three (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: Award 3 for six correct rows, 2 for four or five, 1 for two or three. A row with more than one tick is wrong.

parts.title: SDLC exam 1b
parts.text: State **two** documents that are produced at the end of the **analysis** stage.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): requirements specification; feasibility report / study; description (DFD) of the current system; list of problems of the current system / findings of data collection
scheme.model_answer: 1 Requirements specification. 2 Feasibility report.
scheme.ai_instructions: Do not credit design documents (ERD, data dictionary, test plan) or the user guide.

parts.title: SDLC exam 1c
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the **evaluation** stage for the canteen system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The new system is compared with the requirements specification (1)
- to decide whether it meets the canteen's needs / solves the problems (queues, lost orders) (1)
- user feedback is collected / improvements or further maintenance are identified (1)

Max 2

points.criterion: System is compared with the requirements / objectives
To judge whether it solves the problems or to identify improvements

scheme.model_answer: To compare the finished system with the requirements specification, to check that it really reduces queues and lost orders, and to identify improvements from users' feedback.

parts.title: SDLC exam 1d
parts.text: After the system is in use, three changes are made. Identify the **type of maintenance** for each change.

fields.label: An error that charges some students twice is fixed
The system is changed to work with the school's new payment provider
A feature showing the weekly menu is added at the students' request

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 Corrective (1)
2 Adaptive (1)
3 Perfective (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Corrective 2 Adaptive 3 Perfective

questions.title: Property tax system and the waterfall model
questions.text: A government agency orders a system to calculate a new property tax. The tax rules are **fixed by law** and will not change during development. The agency requires **complete documentation** at every stage. The developer decides to use the **waterfall model**.

parts.title: SDLC exam 2a
parts.text: Give **one** feature of the waterfall model.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): stages are completed one after another in a fixed order / sequential; each stage must be finished (signed off) before the next begins; it is difficult to go back to an earlier stage; documentation is produced at the end of each stage; testing takes place after coding
scheme.model_answer: Each stage is completed and signed off before the next stage begins.

parts.title: SDLC exam 2b
parts.text: Explain **two** reasons why the waterfall model is suitable for this project.

scheme.mark_scheme:
For each reason: identification (1) + explanation linked to the scenario (1). Max 2 reasons.
- Requirements are fixed by law (1) so they can be fully defined at the start and will not need to change later (1)
- Documentation is produced at every stage (1) which meets the agency's requirement for complete documentation (1)
- Clear stages and milestones (1) so the agency can monitor progress / cost and time can be estimated (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 The tax rules are fixed by law, so all requirements can be written at the start and the inflexibility of waterfall is not a problem. 2 Waterfall produces documentation at the end of every stage, which meets the agency's demand for complete documentation.
scheme.ai_instructions: The explanation mark needs a link to the scenario (fixed law, documentation, monitoring). Do not credit the same reason twice.

parts.title: SDLC exam 2c
parts.text: State **two** disadvantages of the waterfall model.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): inflexible — changes are difficult / expensive once a stage is finished; the client sees the working system only at the end; errors are found late (testing after coding); little user involvement during development; not suitable when requirements are unclear or likely to change; long projects may no longer meet users' needs when finished
scheme.model_answer: 1 Changes are hard to make once a stage has been signed off. 2 The client only sees a working system at the end.

parts.title: SDLC exam 2d
parts.text: State the stage of the waterfall model in which errors in the requirements are usually discovered.

scheme.mark_scheme: Testing (stage) (1) — accept: during testing near the end of the project / acceptance testing
scheme.model_answer: The testing stage.

questions.title: Fitness app and the agile model
questions.text: A start-up is developing a **fitness mobile app**. Investors want to see a working version as early as possible, and the features will change as users give feedback. The developers use the **agile model** with **two-week sprints**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The team plans / selects features (user stories) from the backlog for the sprint (1)
- designs, codes and tests these features (1)
- produces a working part (increment) of the app (1)
- which is reviewed by / shown to the client or users for feedback (1)

Max 2

points.criterion: Features are planned / chosen for the sprint
Features are built and tested, producing a working increment reviewed by the client

scheme.model_answer: The team chooses a few features from the backlog, designs, codes and tests them, and at the end shows the working part of the app to the investors for feedback.

parts.title: SDLC exam 3b
parts.text: Analyse **two** advantages of using the agile model for this start-up.

scheme.mark_scheme:
For each advantage: identification (1) + analysis of its effect in the scenario (1). Max 2 advantages.
- Working software is delivered early / after every sprint (1) so investors can see progress quickly / the app can reach users sooner (1)
- Requirements can change between sprints (1) so features can be adapted to users' feedback (1)
- The client / users are involved throughout (1) so the final app better meets their needs (1)
- Problems are found early in each sprint (1) so they are cheaper to fix (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 A working version is produced after every two-week sprint, so investors can see the app early, as they want. 2 Requirements can be changed between sprints, so new features can be added or changed after users give feedback.
scheme.ai_instructions: The second mark of each advantage needs a link to the start-up scenario (investors, user feedback). Do not credit the same advantage twice.

parts.title: SDLC exam 3c
parts.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of the agile model for the **investors**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One disadvantage (1) + explanation (1):
- final cost / completion date are hard to predict (1) because requirements keep changing / the number of sprints is not fixed (1)
- investors must attend reviews regularly (1) which takes a lot of their time (1)
- less documentation (1) so later maintenance may be harder / more expensive (1)
- scope may keep growing (1) increasing cost (1)

points.criterion: Explains its effect on the investors

scheme.model_answer: The total cost and finishing date are hard to predict, because features keep changing after each sprint, so investors cannot be sure how much money they will need.

parts.title: SDLC exam 3d
parts.text: State **one** difference between the agile model and the waterfall model in each of the following.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Client involvement (1): agile — client involved throughout / reviews every sprint; waterfall — mainly at the start and the end

When working software is delivered (1): agile — after every sprint (early and often); waterfall — only at the end of the project

points.criterion: Correct difference in delivery of working software

scheme.model_answer: Client involvement: in agile the client reviews every sprint, in waterfall mainly at the start and end. Delivery: agile delivers working software every sprint, waterfall only at the end.
scheme.ai_instructions: Each answer must refer to both models (or clearly contrast them).

questions.title: Bank payment system and choosing a model
questions.text: A bank is replacing its **online payment system**. The project is **very large and expensive**, the system must be **secure**, and there are many **risks**: new technology, strict security rules and a large number of users. The bank is considering the **waterfall**, **agile** and **spiral** models.

parts.title: SDLC exam 4a
parts.text: Describe the **four** phases of each loop of the spiral model.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One mark per phase described:
1 Determine objectives / requirements / alternatives for this loop (1)
2 Identify and resolve risks — risk analysis, often building a prototype (1)
3 Develop and test the next version / engineering (1)
4 Evaluate (client review) and plan the next iteration / loop (1)

points.criterion: Phase 4: evaluate and plan the next loop

scheme.model_answer: 1 Determine the objectives of the loop. 2 Analyse the risks and reduce them, e.g. with a prototype. 3 Develop and test the next version. 4 The client evaluates it and the next loop is planned.
scheme.ai_instructions: Accept the phases in any wording; one mark per correct phase even if not in order.

parts.title: SDLC exam 4b
parts.text: Explain why the spiral model is suitable for the bank's project.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The project is high-risk / large / expensive (1)
- the spiral model analyses and reduces risks in every loop (e.g. with prototypes) before the full system is built (1)
- security problems can be found early (1)

Max 2

points.criterion: Refers to the high risk / size of the project
Spiral analyses and reduces risks in every loop

scheme.model_answer: The bank's project is large and high-risk, and the spiral model carries out a risk analysis in every loop, so security and technical risks are found and reduced with prototypes before the whole system is built.

parts.title: SDLC exam 4c
parts.text: Discuss which development model — waterfall, agile or spiral — is the most suitable for the bank's project. In your answer analyse the advantages **and** disadvantages of **at least two** models and reach a justified conclusion.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Analysis of models (max 4):
- Waterfall: clear structure, documentation, cost estimated (1); but inflexible, risks and errors found late — dangerous for a security-critical system (1)
- Agile: flexible, early working versions, client feedback (1); but less documentation, unpredictable cost, risk management not central — weak for strict security rules (1)
- Spiral: risk analysis every loop, prototypes reduce risk, suitable for large projects (1); but expensive, needs risk specialists, timescale uncertain (1)

Conclusion (max 2):
- Spiral is most suitable (1)
- justified by the scenario: high risk / security / large and expensive project, so the cost of risk analysis is worth it (1)

Accept another conclusion only if well justified from the scenario.

points.criterion: Clear conclusion naming the most suitable model

scheme.model_answer: Waterfall is easy to manage and well documented, but it is inflexible and testing happens late, so security problems might only be found at the end. Agile delivers working versions early and adapts to change, but it has less documentation and less control of cost and risk. The spiral model analyses risks in every loop and uses prototypes, which suits a large, high-risk system, although it is expensive and needs specialists. The spiral model is the most suitable, because the bank's project is large, expensive and security-critical, so the extra cost of risk analysis is justified.
scheme.ai_instructions: Analysis marks need specific advantages/disadvantages, not just names. Maximum 4 analysis marks and 2 conclusion marks. The justification must use the scenario (risk, security, size, cost).

topic_exam.title: SDLC models — Exam (Paper 2 style)
topic_exam.instructions: Answer **all** questions. The number of marks is given in brackets [ ] at the end of each part. Total: 40 marks. Time: 40 minutes.
